Every cream needs something to give it body, to keep the oils and the water from drifting apart, and to lend the whole thing a smooth, even feel as it goes on. In our formulas that job belongs to tara gum.

Tara gum is a galactomannan, a long-chain sugar molecule, milled from the seed of Caesalpinia spinosa, a small thorny tree native to the Peruvian Andes. The seed is cleaned, milled and dried at low temperature with no solvents involved, so what reaches the bottle is a purified plant powder and nothing else. It is vegetal and non-GMO. You will also have met it in the food aisle, where it thickens sauces and ice cream under the name E417.

It is a large molecule, which matters more than it sounds. A polymer this size sits on the surface of the skin rather than passing into it, and that tells you a good deal about what it can and cannot do.

This is the honest part, and worth reading if you have seen tara gum sold as something grander. You will find it marketed as three things it is not. Follow each claim back to its source and it does not belong to the gum.
So we do not claim them. Tara gum is in our formulas to give them their texture and their stability, and that is how we describe it.

Tara gum appears in every one of our formulations, low in the ingredient list, at a fraction of a percent. On the label it reads as its INCI name, Caesalpinia Spinosa Gum. The exact percentage is published on each product page, as it is for everything else we use.

Tara gum has a long record of safe use in both food and skincare, and an independent expert-panel review of this family of plant gums found no safety concerns at the levels used in cosmetics. It is well tolerated, sits comfortably within a vegan routine, and is gentle enough for the sensitive skin types in the range.

Skin-imaging studies show tara gum can leave a light film on the surface that may help hold a little moisture in the short term. We treat that as a small surface-level extra rather than a headline, the evidence is early, and comes mostly from formulas where tara gum was paired with other ingredients.

Most of what a skincare oil does is quiet work: soften the surface, slow the loss of water, and carry the rest of the formula evenly across the skin. Squalane does that quiet work better than almost anything, and it does it without the weight or the short shelf life of a heavier oil.

Squalane is a lightweight emollient oil, and the way to understand it is through its relationship to squalene. Squalene is a lipid your own skin makes, one of the main components of the film that sits on its surface. It is good at what it does, but it has a weakness: the same chemistry that makes it useful also makes it oxidise quickly, which is why the plant oils richest in it tend to turn.

Squalane is squalene with that weakness taken out. Through hydrogenation, the reactive parts of the molecule are saturated, leaving an oil that is far more stable while keeping the light, skin-friendly feel. Ours is made from olive, Olea europaea, rather than from shark liver, the traditional source and still a live conservation concern. So what reaches the bottle is a plant-derived, stable version of a lipid your skin already recognises.
Squalane is a genuinely good ingredient, which is exactly why the claims around it tend to drift past what the evidence supports. Three in particular are worth correcting.

Take those away and what remains is still substantial: a stable, lightweight emollient that softens the skin, slows water loss, and carries the rest of the formula. That is why it is in every one we make.

Squalane appears in every one of our formulations. Where it falls in the ingredient list depends on how much a given product carries, and that varies by style, so it reads higher in some and lower in others. On the label it is simply Squalane, its INCI name. The exact percentage is published on each product page, as it is for everything we use.

Squalane has one of the longest and cleanest safety records in cosmetics. Independent expert-panel reviews have repeatedly found squalane and squalene safe as used, with no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law. It is non-sensitising, sits as comfortably on oily and blemish-prone skin as on dry, and suits a vegan routine, since ours is olive-derived.

Tamanu oil is pressed from the nut of Calophyllum inophyllum, a tree that grows along the shores of the Pacific and tropical Asia, where its oil has been used on the skin for generations. It is one of the richer conditioning oils in the Dry and Dry Sensitive blends, and one where the traditional reputation and the human evidence sit some distance apart.

Tamanu is a cold-pressed organic oil, thick and green, made up of oleic, linoleic, palmitic and stearic acids along with an unusual set of plant compounds found in few other oils. As an emollient it is genuinely good: rich, cushioning and well suited to drier, harder-worn skin, which is the job it does in our blends.

The rest of its reputation, for healing scars, calming acne and fighting bacteria, comes almost entirely from laboratory work, animal studies and long traditional use. That is interesting, and worth reading about, but it is not the same as being shown to work on human skin, and we keep those two things apart.
Tamanu is sold on some of the boldest claims of any plant oil. The activity behind them is real in the laboratory, but the setting matters.
So we claim the one thing we can stand behind, that it is a rich, conditioning oil, and we describe the rest as the promising, unfinished evidence it is.

Tamanu appears in the Dry Sensitive and Dry blends, high on the ingredient list since it is one of the main oils. On the label it reads by its INCI name, shown with its common name, and marked as cold-pressed and organic. The exact percentage is published on each product page.

Tamanu suits a vegan routine and carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law. One honest caution, though: it is pressed from a tree nut, and there are documented cases of allergic reactions to it, so anyone with a tree-nut allergy should avoid it, and everyone else is wise to patch test before first use. We would rather flag that plainly than tuck it away.

Evening primrose oil is pressed from the small seeds of Oenothera biennis, a wildflower that opens at dusk. It is best known for one particular fatty acid, and for a reputation that runs some way ahead of the evidence, so this is a page where being plain matters.

Evening primrose oil is a cold-pressed organic oil, high in linoleic acid and carrying a share of gamma-linolenic acid, or GLA, an uncommon omega-6 fatty acid that is the reason the oil gets the attention it does. In the skin, linoleic and gamma-linolenic acids both feed into the lipids the barrier is built from, which is the sensible basis for using it in a moisturiser for dry skin.

Where care is needed is with what the studies actually tested. Most of the well-known research gave evening primrose oil as an oral supplement, and that is a different question from what a cold-pressed oil does when you smooth it onto the skin.
This is the honest part, and it matters more here than with most oils. Evening primrose is sold on claims that trace back to studies of a very different kind.
So we keep to what the topical evidence supports: a soft, conditioning oil whose GLA may lend the skin barrier some quiet support. That is the reason it is in the Dry and Dry Sensitive blends.

Evening primrose appears in the Dry Sensitive and Dry blends, high on the ingredient list since it is one of the main oils. On the label it reads by its INCI name, shown with its common name, and marked as cold-pressed and organic. The exact percentage is published on each product page.

Evening primrose oil is well tolerated on the skin and suits a vegan routine. It sits comfortably on sensitive skin, which is why it is part of the Dry Sensitive blend, and as a plant seed oil it carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law.

Baobab oil is pressed from the seed of the African baobab, the broad, ancient tree sometimes called the tree of life. In our formulas it is one of the conditioning oils that give the Dry and Dry Sensitive blends their softness, and it does a plain, useful job well.

Baobab seed oil, Adansonia digitata, is a cold-pressed organic oil made up mostly of oleic, linoleic and palmitic acids, with vitamin E and a share of plant sterols. That balance of fatty acids is what makes it a good emollient: stable, easy-going and quick to soften the skin without feeling heavy.

It is worth being clear about one thing the marketing tends to get wrong. Baobab is often called an omega-3 oil, but the seed oil is really an omega-6 and omega-9 oil, with only a trace of omega-3. That does not make it any less useful, it just makes the usual headline inaccurate, and we would rather describe the oil that is actually in the bottle.
Baobab attracts more than its share of grand language, helped along by the "tree of life" name. Two claims are worth correcting.
What is left is honest and worth having: a stable, conditioning oil that softens the skin and helps it hold moisture, with a small but real study behind that.

Baobab appears in the Dry Sensitive, Dry and Balanced blends, high on the ingredient list since it is one of the main oils. On the label it reads by its INCI name, shown with its common name, and marked as cold-pressed and organic. The exact percentage is published on each product page, as it is for everything we use.

Baobab oil is well tolerated, and in a small controlled study it did not irritate the skin any more than water did. It suits a vegan routine and sits comfortably on sensitive skin, which is why it anchors the Dry Sensitive blend. As a plant seed oil it carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law.

Sea buckthorn oil is pressed from the small, bright orange berries of Hippophae rhamnoides, a hardy shrub of cold coastlines and mountain slopes. It is one of the more distinctive oils in the Dry and Dry Sensitive blends, both for its colour and for an uncommon fatty acid it shares with your own skin.

There are two oils in sea buckthorn, and the difference matters. The seed oil is lighter and richer in the everyday omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids. The fruit oil, which is the one we use, is the deep-orange oil from the berry flesh, and it is unusually high in palmitoleic acid, an omega-7. That is the point of interest, because palmitoleic acid is one of the fatty acids your own skin makes, so the oil reads as familiar to the barrier rather than foreign to it. Alongside it come carotenoids, which give the oil its colour, and tocopherols.

Where care is needed is with the setting of the evidence. Much of the well-known research on sea buckthorn tested it as something you swallow, which is a different question from what a cold-pressed oil does on the surface of the skin.
Sea buckthorn attracts some bold claims, and the compounds behind them are genuinely interesting. The catch is where they were studied.

So we keep to what topical use supports: a conditioning fruit oil whose omega-7 suits the barrier and whose carotenoids lend an antioxidant note. That is why it is in the Dry and Dry Sensitive blends.

Dragon fruit, or pitaya, is the striking fruit of a climbing cactus, Hylocereus undatus. Everyone knows the flesh. What we use is the oil pressed from the small black seeds inside it, and that is a quite different, and rather more useful, thing.

It matters which part of the plant a skincare ingredient comes from, and dragon fruit is the clearest example in our range. The flesh holds the betalains and vitamin C the fruit is celebrated for. The seeds hold oil, and that oil is roughly half linoleic acid, the essential omega-6 the skin draws on to build the lipids of its barrier. Oleic and palmitic acids make up most of the rest, and a genuine load of natural tocopherols comes along too.

That is a strong profile for a moisturiser, and it puts dragon fruit seed oil in the same company as grape seed: light, quick to absorb, and generous with the one fatty acid the skin barrier actually needs. It is the reason the oil appears in four of our five blends.
Dragon fruit is an appealing thing to put on a label, and the marketing tends to reach for the fruit's reputation rather than the seed's chemistry. Two things worth separating.
What we claim is what the oil is: a light, cold-pressed seed oil, high in linoleic acid, carrying its own vitamin E. That needs no help from the fruit's reputation.

Bladderwrack is the brown seaweed you have stepped over on every rocky beach along the north Devon coast, the same species that grows on the rocks below Welcombe. It is our signature ingredient, and the one that gives the whole range its coastal character.

Bladderwrack, Fucus vesiculosus, is a brown seaweed of the north Atlantic. The research on the seaweed itself is genuinely interesting: it is rich in fucoidans, the sulphated polysaccharides unique to brown algae, in phlorotannins, a family of marine polyphenols, and in fucoxanthin, a golden pigment. Most of the antioxidant and soothing activity credited to bladderwrack in the literature belongs to the first two, and both are water-soluble.

That last point shapes what we can honestly say, because we use bladderwrack as a cold, solvent-free infusion in sunflower oil, not as the water-based extract the studies test. The water-soluble fucoidans stay behind, and most of the phlorotannins with them, though the smaller phlorotannins may carry a little way into the oil. What crosses over most reliably is the lipophilic fucoxanthin, and that, with the coastal kinship, is why it is here.

This is the honest part. Bladderwrack is among the most oversold ingredients in skincare, and much of what you will read about it does not survive contact with the form we use, or with the evidence behind it.
What we do say is smaller and honest: a modest antioxidant note, and a real kinship with the coast it belongs to.

Bladderwrack appears in every one of our formulations, near the end of the list, at a fraction of a percent. On the label it reads by its INCI name, shown with its common name. The exact percentage is published on each product page, as it is for everything we use.

Bladderwrack, carried in sunflower oil, is gentle and well tolerated, with a long record of safe cosmetic use and no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law. It suits a vegan routine and sits comfortably on sensitive skin.

Argan oil is pressed from the kernel inside the fruit of the argan tree, which grows only in southwestern Morocco. It is a genuinely good conditioning oil, and also one of the most over-sold, so this is a page that gains from restraint.

Worth noting that the best-known of those studies combined taking argan by mouth with applying it to the skin, so the effect cannot be pinned on the topical oil alone.
Few oils carry as much marketing as argan, "liquid gold" and the rest. The oil is good enough not to need it, so here is the plain version.
So we keep to the honest description: a well-tolerated, vitamin-E-rich conditioning oil with some modest clinical support. That is a good thing to be, and it is what argan is.

Jojoba is the golden liquid pressed from the seed of Simmondsia chinensis, a desert shrub. It behaves like an oil, but chemically it is something more unusual, and that difference is the whole reason it sits so comfortably on the skin.

Jojoba is not, strictly, an oil. It is a liquid wax, made almost entirely of wax esters, and wax esters happen to be one of the main building blocks of your own sebum, the film the skin makes to keep itself supple. Because the two are so alike, jojoba reads as familiar to the skin: it absorbs cleanly, sits lightly even on oilier skin, and softens without the heaviness of a richer oil.

That wax-ester make-up has a second benefit. Where most plant oils will slowly oxidise and turn, jojoba is remarkably stable and keeps for a long time, which is part of why it earns its place in the Dry and Balanced blends.
Jojoba is genuinely useful, so most of what is said about it is fair. Two claims, though, are worth putting straight.
What we do claim is simple and well founded: a light, stable, sebum-like wax that softens the skin and sits comfortably on almost anyone.

The pomegranate is a fruit of several parts, and they are not interchangeable. The peel and juice hold the ellagitannins, the polyphenols behind most of the antioxidant research. The seed, and the oil pressed from it, hold something different: punicic acid, a conjugated fatty acid that is rare in the plant world and gives the seed oil its character. That is the part we use, and it is worth being clear about.

As a conditioning oil it softens and nourishes, and its punicic acid carries an antioxidant and calming character in the research, mostly shown so far in the laboratory rather than on skin.
Pomegranate is one of the most heavily researched fruits in nutrition, and that research gets borrowed freely by skincare. The trouble is that most of it is about the wrong part of the fruit.
So we describe the seed oil for what it is: a conditioning oil with an unusual and interesting fatty acid, and we leave the peel's reputation with the peel.

Grape seed is sold hard on its antioxidants, and the science behind those antioxidants is real. The catch is which form was studied.
So we keep our claim honest and small: a light, quick-absorbing oil that feeds the barrier and suits oilier skin. That is the reason it is here.

Most skincare ingredients act on your skin. Inulin does not. It is food, and the things it feeds are the microbes already living on you. That shift, from treating the skin to feeding what lives on it, is the idea the whole range is built around.

Inulin is a plant fibre, a chain of fructose units, drawn from chicory root. You may know it from nutrition, where it is the fibre that feeds helpful gut bacteria. The skin works on a similar principle, and inulin does a similar job there.

The mechanism is neat. Your skin's helpful residents, Staphylococcus epidermidis and others like it, carry the enzymes to break inulin down and use it as food. Several less welcome species largely do not. So adding inulin is less like intervening and more like laying on a meal that only some of the guests can eat. Feed the ones you want, and they grow, and hold their ground against the ones you do not. That is what "support, not control" means in practice, and inulin is where the idea is most literal.
Microbiome skincare is a field where the marketing has run some way ahead of the evidence, and we are not going to pretend our own prebiotic is above that.

So we describe the mechanism, which is real and well characterised in the laboratory, and we stop short of promising an outcome nobody has yet demonstrated on human skin. It is a good idea with good foundations, and that is worth saying without overstating it.

Inulin appears in every one of our formulations, toward the end of the ingredient list, which is where you would expect a prebiotic used at a low level. On the label it reads simply as Inulin. The exact percentage is published on each product page.

Inulin is a plant fibre with an excellent safety record, well tolerated on sensitive skin, and suitable for a vegan routine. It carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law. Being food for microbes rather than an active on the skin, it is about as gentle an ingredient as we use.

Barley is malted and fermented to make the alcohol that becomes gin. The gin is distilled off, and what is left behind is a great deal of spent grain. This ingredient is made from that. It is the part of the process nobody wanted, and it turns out to be rather good at holding water in skin.

Spring barley is grown in East Anglia, malted, and fermented with Saccharomyces, brewer's yeast. The alcohol is distilled off to make gin. The fermented grain that remains, which would otherwise be waste, is captured fresh and filtered, and that filtrate is what reaches our formulas. It is made in the UK, and it carries the certification for genuinely upcycled materials rather than merely claiming the word.

What the fermenting does is break the barley down into smaller, more soluble pieces: free amino acids, peptides, sugars, phenolics. That is what a postbiotic is. Not live cultures, which could not survive in a jar on your shelf, but the useful residue of a fermentation that has already finished.

One thing worth knowing, because it is the sort of thing that never gets said. The material we buy is half barley ferment and half glycerin. So a portion of the glycerin on our label arrives inside this ingredient rather than being added separately. Both are declared. We mention it because you would have no way of knowing otherwise, and because the two work together: the glycerin pulls water in, and the ferment seems to help hold on to it.
The evidence for this ingredient is better than we expected. The marketing around it still runs ahead in a few places.

What we are left with is a humectant with real, if small, evidence behind it, made from something that would otherwise have been thrown away. That is a good ingredient. It does not need the antioxidants and the minerals bolted on.

The barley ferment appears in every one of our formulations, in the middle of the ingredient list. It reads by its INCI name, Saccharomyces/Barley Seed Ferment Filtrate, which is a mouthful and means barley fermented by yeast and then filtered. Note that it arrives with an equal weight of glycerin, so part of the glycerin declared further up the list comes in with this ingredient. The exact percentages are published on each product page.

The filtrate contains no live organisms, suits a vegan routine, and carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law. It is certified upcycled, conforms to the COSMOS organic standard, is certified under NaTrue, and is palm-free. It is derived from barley, a cereal, so if you are sensitive to cereals a patch test first is sensible. Note that this is a question about your skin, not about coeliac disease, which concerns what you eat rather than what you put on it.

Of all the ingredients on our label, this is the one we most underestimated. It has no scent, no colour, no story, and it does not sound like anything. What it does is hold the product at the acidity your skin needs, and that is a bigger deal than most of the things brands put on the front of a bottle.

Healthy skin is mildly acidic, sitting at around pH 5. This is not a quirk. It is how the skin works. The enzymes that build the barrier's lipids only function properly in acid conditions. The enzymes that break the barrier down speed up as things turn alkaline. And the microbes you want on your skin prefer acid, while the ones you do not prefer neutral: the research shows Staphylococcus epidermidis, the helpful resident, grows contentedly at pH 4.7, while Staphylococcus aureus, which you would rather not encourage, does best nearer neutral. Even the antimicrobial peptide your own skin makes works far better in acid than out of it.

Which means the pH of anything you leave on your skin is not a technicality. A cream that sits at the wrong acidity is nudging your barrier enzymes, your lipid production and your microbiome in the wrong direction, quietly, every day. Ours is built to sit where your skin already is, and sodium citrate is the buffer that holds it there, not just on the day it was made but through a shelf life, as things shift and settle.

It has a second job as well. Trace metals get into every formula, and they catalyse the oxidation that turns oils rancid. Sodium citrate binds them up. That keeps the oils good, and since oxidised oils are irritating to skin, it keeps them from bothering you too.
Sodium citrate is too plain to attract much nonsense, but there are two claims worth handling, and one of them is a claim we could have made ourselves.

So: an ingredient that holds the product at the acidity your skin already wants, and keeps the oils from turning while it does. It will never be on the front of a bottle. It is one of the most consequential things in it.

Sodium citrate appears in every one of our formulations, and it sits higher in the list than you might expect for something so anonymous. That is deliberate: holding a pH steady over a shelf life takes a real amount rather than a token pinch, and it also works alongside the gluconolactone, which needs a mildly acidic product to preserve properly. Skin pH, preservative pH and oil stability all want the same thing, which is a piece of luck we will happily take. The exact percentage is published on each product page.

Sodium citrate has been assessed by the independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients and found safe as used, and it has a long record as a food additive besides. It suits a vegan routine, sits comfortably on sensitive skin, and carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law.

Gluconolactone is made by fermenting glucose. It is a gentle system, well tolerated, and accepted under the organic cosmetic standards, which is why we chose it over the harsher options.

It has a useful second property. Gluconolactone carries several hydroxyl groups, and each one attracts water, so it works as a humectant at the same time. Most preservatives do nothing for your skin. Now the part that needs care. Gluconolactone belongs to the polyhydroxy acid family, the PHAs, and PHAs are well known as gentle exfoliants. At that level it is not resurfacing your skin, and we would rather tell you that than let three flattering letters do work they have not earned.
One of these corrections is aimed at us, which is a first for these pages, and it is the more important of the two.
So: a gentle, fermentation-derived preservative that also holds a little water. That is a good, honest thing for an ingredient to be, and it is what this one is.

Chlorella is a single-celled green microalga, and the version in our formulas is a particular one: an active built from compounds in the algal cell wall, made in Barcelona from algae grown in sealed tanks. There is very little of it in the bottle. That deserves an explanation rather than a shrug, so here is one.

The chlorella is grown in closed photobioreactors, sealed vessels rather than open ponds, then the cell walls are opened in water and the useful compounds are separated out and purified. What results is a concentrate: not ground-up algae, but a standardised set of active molecules, held at a fixed strength.

Here is the part worth being straight about. That concentrate is only a small fraction of the liquid it is supplied in, and we use that liquid at one percent. Do the arithmetic and the chlorella extract in your jar works out at roughly eight thousandths of one percent. Written down, that sounds like nothing.

The reason it is not nothing is that this is exactly the strength every study used. The maker tested the material at between a third of a percent and one percent, and we use it at one percent, the top of that range. So the chlorella concentration in our jar is the same as the chlorella concentration in the studies. The number that means something is the one percent, not the eight thousandths, and any brand telling you otherwise is either confused or hoping you are.
Now the honest part, and here we part company a little with the people who make this ingredient.

What is left is an interesting, carefully made active with real but limited evidence, used at the strength it was tested at. That is a fair description. It is the one we will stand by until somebody outside the company that sells it does the work.

Chlorella appears in every one of our formulations, near the end of the ingredient list. It arrives inside a one percent active, and the rest of that active is water, propanediol to carry it and a trace of lactic acid to hold it at the right acidity. All of them are on the label, which is why propanediol sits higher up the list than the chlorella it brought with it. Each has its own page here, because we would rather show you how the parts fit together than leave you wondering.

This is one of the few ingredients in our range with human safety data behind it at the exact strength we use. The maker patch tested it on fifty volunteers at one percent: not irritating, not sensitising. It is certified vegan by the Vegan Society, approved under the COSMOS and NATRUE organic standards, and free of nuts, gluten and other common allergens. The algae are grown in sealed tanks rather than gathered, so nothing is taken from the wild. It is a freshwater microalga with no connection at all to our coast, which we mention only because it would be easy to imply otherwise.

Some ingredients you choose. Some arrive because they came in the bottle with something else. Propanediol is the second kind, and when we sat down to write about it we assumed there would be nothing to say. We were wrong, and the correction is worth reading.

Propanediol is a clear liquid made by fermentation. It is in our formulas because our chlorella active is supplied as a liquid, and propanediol is about a third of that liquid: it dissolves the algal compounds, keeps them stable and keeps the bottle free of microbes. Take it away and there is no chlorella to add. That is how it got here, and for a while it was the only thing we thought it was doing.

It does two other things, and both of them touch your skin. It is a genuine humectant, which means it attracts water and holds it in the skin's surface, in much the same way glycerin does but with a lighter feel. And it is a penetration enhancer, which means it makes the outer skin a little more willing to let water-loving ingredients through. That second one is quietly useful in a formula like ours, where several of the ingredients that matter are water-soluble and need to reach somewhere to be worth anything.

One thing worth knowing, since the two get muddled. Propanediol is not propylene glycol. They sound alike, they are different molecules, and propanediol is the gentler of the two.
Propanediol takes it from both directions: condemned as a nasty chemical by one crowd, oversold as a hydrating active by another. Both are wrong.

So: a fermentation-derived carrier that holds water in your skin and helps the rest of the formula get where it is going. Less glamorous than an oil, and considerably more useful than we first gave it credit for.

Propanediol appears in every one of our formulations at around three tenths of a percent, which is why it sits where it does in the list. If you have wondered why a name you do not recognise ranks above ingredients you do, this is your answer: our chlorella active is largely propanediol, and every part of it is declared. The exact percentage is published on each product page.

Propanediol has a good safety record and is well tolerated on sensitive skin. Within our chlorella active it is certified vegan by the Vegan Society and approved under the COSMOS and NATRUE organic standards. It is made by fermentation rather than from petroleum, and it carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law.

Lactic acid is one of the best known ingredients in skincare. It is an alpha hydroxy acid, and at the right strength it loosens dead cells and smooths the surface of the skin. Our products contain roughly one part in fifty thousand of it, which is nowhere near enough to do any of that. So why is it on the label at all?

The answer is unglamorous, which is rather the point. Our chlorella active is supplied as a liquid, and that liquid has to be held at a particular acidity or the algal compounds in it are not stable. A small amount of lactic acid is what holds it there. Its maker lists the function in one phrase: pH modifier. It makes up a fraction of a percent of that active, and the active makes up one percent of our formula. Multiply the two together and you get about two thousandths of one percent.

At that level it is not doing anything to your skin. It is not exfoliating, not smoothing, not brightening. It finished its work before the ingredient ever reached our workshop, inside the bottle it arrived in. It is on our label because everything is on our label, including the parts that are not working for you.
This page exists because of one of the quieter tricks of the industry, and lactic acid is the ideal place to explain it.

So no, our products do not exfoliate, and the lactic acid on the label is not evidence that they do. It is evidence that we list everything. Those are two very different things, and we would rather you knew which one you were looking at.

Lactic acid is the last ingredient on every one of our lists, which is exactly where a trace belongs. Ingredient lists are ordered by how much of each thing is in the product, so the bottom of the list is the honest place to look for what is barely there. The exact percentage is published on each product page, as it is for everything we use.

Lactic acid is made by fermenting plant sugars, suits a vegan routine, and carries no restrictions at this level under UK or EU cosmetic law. At around two thousandths of a percent it presents no irritation concern of any kind, including for sensitive skin. The research shows lactic acid is well tolerated even at the far higher levels used in exfoliating products, and ours is nowhere near those.

This ingredient does two useful things and raises one awkward question, and since the question is about the thing this whole brand is built on, it would be cowardly to leave it out.

Glyceryl caprylate is made by joining glycerin to caprylic acid, both from plant oils. On the skin it is an emollient: it softens, and it helps the formula spread and feel the way it does. That alone would earn it a place.

It also makes life difficult for microbes, by disrupting their membranes. It could not preserve a cream by itself, but alongside the gluconolactone and the sodium benzoate it means the whole preservative system can be gentler than it would otherwise need to be. That is a genuine benefit, and it is part of why these formulas suit reactive skin.

And now the awkward part. A preservative does not stop working when you take the cream out of the jar. It goes onto your skin, and it stays active there for a while, and your skin is where your microbiome lives. We are a brand built on supporting that microbiome. It would be strange not to ask what our own preservatives are doing to it.

The honest answer is that we do not fully know. The research shows this matters: some preservative systems hold back the troublesome species while leaving the helpful ones alone, and others suppress the helpful ones as well. We chose about the gentlest system available to us, and we chose it deliberately. But nobody has tested our particular combination on a human microbiome, and until somebody does, we are not going to tell you it is fine. We will tell you we thought about it, we made the most careful choice we could, and the question remains open.
Two claims get made around ingredients like this one. The first is dishonest. The second is one we would love to make and will not.

What we are left with is an emollient that softens your skin, and a preservative that helps keep the product from going off, chosen to be as gentle as we could manage, with an honest question mark over the thing we care most about. That is where the evidence leaves us, so that is where we are going to stand.

Oil and water do not mix. Every moisturiser ever made is an argument with that fact, and the emulsifier is what wins it. Ours is made from olive, it is in every formula we make, and it is the least discussed and most important ingredient in the bottle.

Cetearyl Olivate and Sorbitan Olivate are two names for one material. They arrive together, they cannot be bought separately, and they work as a pair, so we have written about them as one thing. Both are made by taking the fatty acids of olive oil and rearranging them chemically onto a sugar-derived backbone. The result is an emulsifier: a molecule with one end that likes oil and one end that likes water, which parks itself at the boundary and holds the two together.

There is a second, subtler property. As the cream cools, these molecules organise themselves into stacked, layered sheets, a structure called a liquid crystal. Those layers happen to resemble the way the lipids in the outer layer of your skin are arranged. That similarity is the reason this system is preferred by formulators who care about mildness: the research suggests such emulsions tend to sit alongside the skin's own structure rather than stripping it, and they give a cushioned finish rather than a greasy one.

It is also free of PEGs, non-ionic, and approved under the organic cosmetic standards. We chose it deliberately. But choosing it well is not the same as being able to claim everything that gets claimed for it, and the next section is about that.
Here is where a great deal of nonsense attaches to a perfectly good ingredient, and some of it is quite hard to dislodge.

What is left is more than enough. It is a mild, PEG-free, olive-derived emulsifier that builds a structure resembling the skin's own, and it is the reason every one of our creams holds together and feels the way it does. It does not need to borrow anything from a bottle of olive oil.

The two olivates appear in every one of our formulations, sitting high in the ingredient list because there is a fair amount of them: an emulsifier has structural work to do and cannot be sprinkled in. You will see them under their INCI names, Cetearyl Olivate and Sorbitan Olivate. They are one material, listed twice, because the law asks for the parts rather than the trade name. The independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients has assessed the sorbitan esters, this pair included, and found them safe as used, both in its original report and again on re-review. That is class-level evidence from a neutral body, which is the strongest kind available here. The material is non-ionic and mild, suits a vegan routine, and carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law. It is also approved as a raw material under the organic cosmetic standards.

One honest note. A worry sometimes raised about sorbitan esters and allergy actually concerns a different member of the family, sorbitan sesquioleate, which is used in fragrances. Carrying that caution across to this ester without naming the culprit would overstate the risk, so we are naming it.

Of all the things people write to skincare brands about, this is near the top: there is alcohol in your moisturiser. It is a fair question and it has a good answer, so here it is properly rather than in a footnote.

The word alcohol covers a very large family of molecules, and the members behave nothing alike. The ones that dry your skin are small and volatile: ethanol, isopropyl alcohol, the thing labelled alcohol denat. They evaporate quickly, and they take some of your skin's moisture with them, which is exactly why they are used in toners and hand gels and why they are worth thinking twice about in a leave-on product.

On the skin it behaves like the other emollients in the formula: it softens, it smooths, and it helps hold moisture in. It is in the same broad chemical family as ethanol in roughly the way a whale is in the same family as a mouse.

It also does structural work. Cetearyl alcohol is much of the reason a cream has body rather than sloshing about, and it helps the emulsifier keep the oil and water together. If you like how a moisturiser feels, this is one of the ingredients you are liking.
This is the ingredient we are asked about most, and the misunderstanding is entirely reasonable. It is also complete.

Vetiver root oil carries a set of identified antioxidant compounds, the vetivones chief among them, and the studies that found them tested the same steam-distilled root oil we use rather than some adjacent material. That is rarer than it sounds.

Vetiver is a tall tussock grass, a cousin of sorghum and lemongrass, and the aromatic part of it is underground. The leaves smell of very little. The roots, which grow downward in a dense fibrous mass rather than spreading sideways, hold the oil, and getting it out is slow work. The roots are dug, washed, dried, and then steam is passed through them for six hours or more, because the oil sits deep in the root tissue and has to diffuse out. A tonne of roots yields a few kilos of oil. It is one of the reasons vetiver is so expensive.

What comes off the still is thick, brown, and slow to pour, and it smells earthy and woody with a smoky edge that some people take a while to warm to. Chemically it is unusual. Most essential oils are dominated by one or two compounds, whereas vetiver runs to well over a hundred, almost all of them sesquiterpenes, with no single constituent accounting for much more than a tenth of the whole. That complexity is why perfumers use it as a base note and why it has taken analytical chemists decades to map it properly.

Ours is an organic oil from Java, distilled from roots grown there, and it goes into every product in the range at between one and three parts in a thousand. On the label it is Vetiveria Zizanioides Root Oil.

Allantoin has been used on skin for over a century, it appears in an enormous number of products, and almost nobody talks about it. That is partly because it does not announce itself. Nothing tingles, nothing glows. It simply makes skin less cross.

Allantoin is the compound that gives comfrey its long reputation as a healing plant, though ours is made synthetically rather than extracted, which gives a purer and more consistent material without the rest of the plant coming along for the ride.

What it does is calm. It settles redness and irritation, and part of how it works is neat: it binds up irritating substances so they cannot reach the skin and provoke it. Regulators in the United States formally recognise it as a skin protectant, which is a stronger position than most cosmetic ingredients ever reach and reflects how well established the evidence is.

It also softens rough skin, by loosening the keratin that holds dead cells together so they shed more readily. That is a different and gentler mechanism than an acid uses, which is why it suits skin too reactive for exfoliation. At the level we use it, expect a quiet smoothing rather than anything dramatic.
Allantoin needs less correcting than most ingredients on this site, which is a pleasant change. Two things are still worth being careful about.

What is left is genuinely good: a well-evidenced soother that calms irritation and softens rough skin, doing its work without fanfare. It is one of the ingredients we are least tempted to overclaim, because it does not need it.

Allantoin appears in every one of our formulations, toward the end of the ingredient list, at a fraction of a percent. That is not a token amount, it is where allantoin actually works: most products use it between a tenth and half a percent, and the evidence sits comfortably in that range. The exact percentage is published on each product page.

Allantoin is one of the least irritating ingredients in cosmetic use. The independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients has assessed it and found it safe as used, and it has a century of use behind it with remarkably little trouble. It suits a vegan routine and carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law. It sits comfortably on sensitive and reactive skin, which is exactly why it is in every formula we make rather than only the gentle ones.

Passion fruit is a superfruit, and the seed oil arrives carrying the fruit's reputation. What is in the bottle is a light golden oil that is roughly three-quarters linoleic acid. That is a useful thing to be, and it is why the oil sits in the oily formulas rather than the dry ones.

Passion seed oil is pressed from the seed of Passiflora edulis, the passion fruit, grown in Peru. It is cold pressed and then filtered, with no heat and no solvents, and what comes out is a single ingredient: 100% passion seed oil, and nothing added to it.

Its character is almost entirely a matter of fatty acids. Independent analysis puts linoleic acid at around 73% of the oil, with oleic acid near 16% and palmitic acid near 9%. Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid, which means skin cannot manufacture it and has to be given it, and it is the direct precursor of the acylceramides that hold the outer barrier together. An oil this high in it is thin, absorbs quickly, and leaves a lighter finish than a richer, more oleic oil would.

The same chemistry is also the oil's weakness. Fatty acids with more than one double bond oxidise readily, and an oil that has turned is more irritating than a fresh one, so this is a material that wants an antioxidant beside it, cool dark storage, and a shelf life that respects both. The supplier gives it eighteen months. The faint gold colour comes from the tocopherols and carotenoids that survive cold pressing, which help a little on that front, though not enough to rely on.

There is a large scientific literature on passion fruit seed, and almost none of it is about the pressed oil. Two things separate them: which fraction of the seed was extracted, and whether the study fed it to people or applied it to skin.

None of that makes the oil less useful. It makes it a different material from the extract. What is in these formulas is an emollient with a good fatty-acid profile, doing an unglamorous job in the ranges that suit it, and that is the whole of the case for it.

Passion seed oil appears in six of the fifteen July formulations, all of them in the Oily and Oily Sensitive ranges. It runs at a supporting level rather than as a base oil, and it climbs through the range: least in the lightest formula, most in the richest, with each Sensitive version carrying more of it than its counterpart. The exact percentage for every product is published on that product's page.

The independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients assessed 244 plant-derived fatty acid oils, passion seed oil among them, and concluded they are safe as used in cosmetics, with the pressed and refined oils in that group showing no signal as skin irritants or sensitisers. The supplier's safety data sheet agrees, and its allergen declaration records none present. The oil suits a vegan routine and sits comfortably on sensitive skin. Comedogenicity has not been formally assessed for this oil, so we do not describe it as non-comedogenic. The one caution worth naming is age: a linoleic-rich oil that has oxidised is more irritating than a fresh one, which is why it is kept cool and dark and given an eighteen-month shelf life.

What matters about it is the fatty acid profile: the specification runs from 67.8 to 83.2 per cent linoleic acid, with oleic a distant second. In our formulas it is a light lipid, in the oil phase of everything except the Balanced range.

Safflower is a daisy-family crop grown for its seed. The oil is pressed cold from that seed, filtered, and supplied at 100 per cent with no solvent, carrier or preservative added. Chemically it is a triglyceride, a matrix of fatty acids, and in this case a very particular one: 67.8 to 83.2 per cent linoleic acid, 8.4 to 21.3 per cent oleic, and the remainder palmitic and stearic. Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid, which means the body cannot synthesise it and has to take it in. Skin uses it structurally, esterified into the acylceramides that hold the barrier's lipid layers in order.

There is a small fraction of other material in there too, tocopherols and phenolic compounds, and it is worth being clear about the scale of it. The published measurements put the phenolics at 141 to 413 milligrams per kilogram of oil, varying more than twofold with genotype and growing season. At the levels we use the oil, that arrives in the finished cream at one or two parts per million. It is real, and it is not a mechanism. The more consequential thing about an oil that is two thirds to four fifths polyunsaturated is that it is prone to oxidation, which is one reason it goes in at modest levels rather than as the bulk of the oil phase.
Safflower is sold hard, and mostly on one number. Three of the claims that travel with it are worth unpicking, because in each case the evidence belongs to something other than the pressed seed oil.

None of which makes it a poor ingredient. It is a clean, well-tolerated, linoleic-rich emollient with a long safety record and a settled regulatory position, and that is what it is here to be. It is simply not the active it gets sold as.

Safflower seed oil is in twelve of our fifteen formulations. It appears in every Flow, Core and Deep built for dry, dry sensitive, oily and oily sensitive skin, and in none of the three Balanced products. Where it is used, the level rises with the weight of the product, from a little under one and a half per cent in the lightest Flow to about five and a half in the heaviest Deep, and the formulas for oilier skin carry more of it than the dry ones, because those formulas lean on lighter oils rather than heavier ones. The exact percentage for each product is published on its own page.

The independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients assessed safflower seed oil alongside 243 other plant-derived fatty acid oils and found the class safe in the present practices of use and concentration. Two human repeat insult patch tests, one at 5 per cent across 214 people and one at 30 per cent across 107, found it neither an irritant nor a sensitiser. It is not classified as hazardous under CLP, and the supplier's allergen statement returns 0.000 per cent for all 81 listed cosmetic allergens. It is a pressed plant oil, so it suits a vegan routine. One thing worth knowing: safflower is in the daisy family, and cross-reactivity within that family is a recognised issue, though it belongs to the flowers and aerial parts rather than to the pressed seed oil. Rice bran oil is pressed from the bran of the rice grain, the papery outer layer that milling takes off. It is a mid-weight conditioning oil, and in our range it does one job rather than several. It appears in three of our fifteen formulations, all of them in the Balanced range.

Bran is everything milling removes from the outside of a rice grain: the seed coat, the aleurone layer beneath it and the germ. It is the part of the grain where most of the interesting chemistry lives, and pressing it gives a fixed oil. Ours is cold pressed from organic Indian rice bran and then filtered, with no solvents and no refining step. That last point shows on the bench: the oil arrives orange-red with a nutty smell, where a refined cooking grade would be pale yellow and neutral. The colour is the part a refinery takes out.

Most of the oil, as with any plant oil, is triglyceride: roughly a third to three fifths oleic acid, a quarter to two fifths linoleic acid, and a tenth to a quarter palmitic. Oleic acid is what makes an oil feel soft and cushioning. Linoleic acid is the one skin uses as a precursor for acylceramides, the lipids that hold the barrier together. Those proportions are given as specification ranges rather than a measured figure for a particular batch, so they are best read as a band.

The rest, a few per cent, is the unsaponifiable fraction, meaning the part of the oil that will not turn into soap. Rice bran oil carries a relatively generous one, and it is what the ingredient is usually sold on: gamma-oryzanol, a family of ferulic acid esters; tocopherols and tocotrienols, the vitamin E family; phytosterols; and a small amount of squalene. Cold pressing keeps more of that fraction in the oil than refining would. How much more is not stated. The specification gives ranges and does not quantify the oryzanol, which is why the antioxidant character sits in the supporting cast on this page rather than at the top of it.

Rice bran oil is sold on a longer list of virtues than the pressed oil can carry. Nearly all of them are genuine findings attached to something else: an isolated constituent, an alcohol extract of the bran, or a rice ferment. Three come up often enough to be worth handling.

What survives all that is an oil that softens skin, holds a little more water in it, and carries a modest antioxidant fraction along for the ride. That is a shorter list than the marketing runs to. It is the list the evidence carries.

Rice bran oil is in three of our fifteen formulations, and all three are in the Balanced range: Flow Balanced, Core Balanced and Deep Balanced. It appears nowhere else. On a Balanced label it sits in the middle of the list, just after the emulsifier, and the level steps up from Flow to Core to Deep. It is there as a supporting oil rather than a base, and the exact percentage is published on each product page.

This oil is in the Balanced formulations because that is where the fit is best. Balanced skin is neither notably dry nor notably oily, and rice bran oil reads in the literature as a good light-to-medium conditioning oil for exactly that: enough cushion to be worth having, not so much that it weighs a formula down. It runs between about a third and three fifths oleic acid, which is what gives it the soft feel, and the same oleic content is why the level is kept low rather than made the base. On oily or breakout-prone skin its comedogenicity is rated low but not zero, and on an already compromised barrier a high-oleic oil can act as a mild penetration enhancer. The independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients has assessed rice bran oil as safe as used, and formulations containing between about 1% and 8% of it were neither irritating nor sensitising in clinical testing, a band all three of our products sit inside. It suits a vegan routine and carries no restrictions under UK or EU cosmetic law.

There is a soothing signal in the literature that we have deliberately not given a card. Delta-tocotrienol isolated from rice bran quietens inflammatory messengers in cell models, tocotrienol reduces mast-cell degranulation in animal work, and gamma-oryzanol is described in similar terms. All of it is isolated constituents and animal studies rather than the pressed oil on human skin, which is a long way from a claim.

Avocado oil is one of the largest oil inclusions anywhere in the range, and it sits only in the Dry and Dry Sensitive creams. It is pressed from the flesh of the fruit rather than the stone, and it is rich, heavy and slow to sink in. On dry skin, that is the whole point.

Nearly every oil in our formulas is pressed from a seed. This one is not. Avocado oil comes from the flesh of the fruit, the green part you would eat, pressed cold and then filtered. Nothing is added and nothing is stripped out. Ours is pressed from organically grown fruit in Kenya and arrives as a single-ingredient material: 100% Persea Gratissima Oil, with no solvent, no preservative and no carrier oil behind it.

What comes out of the press is mostly triglycerides, and the fatty acids sitting on them decide how the oil behaves. Analysis of our supplied lot puts oleic acid at about 60%, palmitic at 17% and linoleic at 9%. Alongside the triglycerides is a small unsaponifiable fraction: phytosterols, tocopherols, carotenoids, and the chlorophyll that gives a cold-pressed avocado oil its green. That chlorophyll is also why the oil dislikes daylight, and one of several reasons our bottles are opaque.

A good deal of the published work on avocado concerns the peel, the stone, or an extract of one of them rather than the pressed flesh oil, and those findings have a habit of migrating across. Three claims are worth untangling.

What survives all of that is still worth having. A rich, well-tolerated oil that softens dry skin and slows the water leaving it, at a level high enough to be felt. That is what the evidence supports, and it is what these six formulas are built on.

Avocado oil appears in six of our fifteen July formulations, all of them Dry or Dry Sensitive, and it sits high in the list on every one. It is one of the largest oil inclusions anywhere in the range, which is deliberate: a rich oil at a token level does not change how a cream feels, and this one is doing structural work. The balanced and oily formulas carry none of it at all, because the weight that helps dry skin is the same weight that oilier skin does not want. Exact percentages are published on each product page.

Avocado oil has been assessed by the independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients and found safe as used. Patch tested in formulations at up to 10.7%, and neat at 100%, it was neither an irritant nor a sensitiser. The one signal on the record is an old case report of a positive patch test to undiluted avocado oil, set against twenty negative controls, so a reaction is possible and uncommon. It suits a vegan routine.

Two things belong here rather than further down the page. Avocado is part of what allergists call latex-fruit syndrome: one of its proteins, Pers a 1, cross-reacts with natural rubber latex, so someone with a significant latex allergy can react to avocado. Cold pressing and filtration lower the protein content of an oil considerably, and refining largely removes it, but if latex or avocado is something you react to, these six products are not for you. Avocado is not a tree nut. Our supplier's site does handle nuts, peanuts, gluten and other food allergens elsewhere in the building, declared as factory presence rather than as anything in the material itself.

The second concerns the oil rather than the fruit. It is high in oleic acid and low in linoleic, and the review literature is consistent that oils in that shape can unsettle a barrier that is already compromised. On intact dry skin it is comfortable. On broken, cracked or inflamed skin, leave it alone. Whether it blocks pores has never been settled by a validated test, which is part of why we keep it to the Dry and Dry Sensitive formulas. And its triglycerides can act as a food source for Malassezia, a yeast that lives on everyone's skin, so if you already avoid oils for that reason, avoid this one too.

The unsaponifiable fraction does a little more than sit there. Phytosterols are structurally similar to the cholesterol skin makes for itself, and the plant-oil review literature credits avocado with a possible soothing effect through them. Possible is the honest word. There is no trial on avocado oil alone to put behind it, so it stays a mechanism rather than a claim, and it is not one of the reasons the oil is in the formula.

Citric acid is one of the most widely used ingredients in food, pharmacy and cosmetics, and it belongs to the alpha hydroxy acid family. That family membership is where most of the confusion starts. In a product held at the acidity of skin, it is not doing the work an AHA is famous for. It is setting the pH and binding metals, which are duller sentences and more useful jobs.

Citric acid is a small organic acid with three acid groups on it, and those three groups are most of why it is useful. The commercial material is not squeezed out of fruit. It is made by microbial fermentation, classically with the mould Aspergillus niger growing on a sugar substrate, a route industrialised somewhere around 1916 to 1919 and largely unchanged in principle since. What arrives is a colourless, odourless crystalline powder that dissolves readily in water.

Three acid groups means three points at which the molecule gives up or takes back a proton, and that is what makes it a buffer rather than simply an acid. It can push a formula down to a chosen acidity and then hold its ground when something tries to push it back. Put it with sodium citrate, which is its own salt, and the pair forms a citrate buffer: more stubborn than either alone, and gentler than the acid on its own. It also sequesters trace metal ions, iron and copper among them, which is a second and quite separate use.

The thing worth understanding about citric acid is that what it does depends almost entirely on where the pH sits. In its free acid form at low pH, like other alpha hydroxy acids, it loosens the bonds between surface skin cells and speeds their shedding. As the pH climbs towards and past its own dissociation points, more of it exists as citrate salt, and that action falls away. The exfoliating benefit and the stinging share the same lever. Our formulas sit between pH 5 and 6, which is roughly where skin sits, and at that acidity citric acid is a pH ingredient and a chelator rather than an exfoliant. The research that supports the exfoliating and structural claims was produced at 20%, or at a pH the papers never recorded.

Citric acid is an alpha hydroxy acid, and that single fact carries an enormous amount of marketing behind it. Much of the science underneath is real. It was just produced under conditions that have little to do with a leave-on product at the acidity of skin: a different concentration, a different pH, or a different material altogether.

None of this is an argument against the ingredient. It is an argument about conditions. Change the pH and raise the concentration and citric acid does become an exfoliating acid, with everything that comes with that, including the sting and the caution about sunlight. Held where we hold it, it is doing quieter chemistry, and that is the version of it described on this page.

Citric acid does not appear on a Biotaderm ingredients list, because it is not added as a formula ingredient. It is used during manufacture, in very small quantities, to bring each batch to its working pH.

Its salt, sodium citrate, is a formula ingredient, and it sits high in every list at a published percentage. The difference between the two is worth understanding. Reaching an acidity takes almost nothing. Holding it steady across a shelf life takes a real amount, and that is the salt's job rather than the acid's.

The independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients assessed citric acid and its salts and found them safe as used, and repeated-insult patch testing at 4% produced no irritation and no sensitisation. True contact allergy to citric acid is uncommon. It suits a vegan routine, and UK and EU cosmetic law places no concentration restriction on it. You will sometimes see 4% quoted as its legal ceiling, which it is not: that figure is the highest leave-on level the panel found in use when it surveyed the market, a description rather than a cap, and the same panel noted that citric acid is chemically and biologically distinct from the alpha hydroxy acids that do carry recommended limits. What genuinely governs tolerance here is concentration and pH together. Severe facial burns have been reported from a 10% peel, and one comparative study found citric acid more irritating than lactic acid on sensitive skin. At buffer levels in a product held between pH 5 and 6 that risk is low, and the same chemistry that makes it mild at low dose is what makes it sharp at high dose and low pH.

One quieter point, at its real weight. Skin's own surface is mildly acidic, and the research shows that acidity supports the enzymes that build the barrier's lipids, restrains the enzymes that break the barrier down, and tips the surface balance towards the microbes that prefer acid. An acid that holds a product in that band is working with all three rather than against them. The direct human evidence is thinner than the mechanism, though. The study that sits closest to our pH used cotton textiles treated with citric acid, worn against the skin for two weeks, and it lowered surface pH and improved barrier measures. That is a treated fabric rather than a cream, which is why this sits here as a supporting note and not as a claim.

["Sodium hydroxide is a strong base, and the job it is given is to meet citric acid in the water phase and take the batch up to the acidity the formula is specified at. It is dosed to an endpoint rather than to a recipe: the correct quantity is whatever titrates that particular batch to target, which for a leave-on at pH 5 to 6 is a fraction of a percent and often well under a tenth of one. The independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients describes the inorganic hydroxides as functioning in cosmetics primarily as pH adjusters, and the acid-base chemistry underneath is textbook.","This is the part that gets inverted. A strong base has no conjugate pair, so sodium hydroxide contributes no buffer capacity whatever; it is the titrant, not the buffer. What it does is convert citric acid step by step into its sodium salts, and those are what hold the pH steady afterwards. Reaching pH 5 to 6 takes roughly 1.7 to 2.2 moles of sodium hydroxide per mole of citric acid, which puts the finished system close to a disodium citrate buffer, generated in the vessel rather than weighed in. Adding sodium hydroxide to citric acid, and weighing in citric acid alongside pre-formed sodium citrate, produce the same solution at the same pH and the same total citrate. ["It is lye, and it is not in the face cream. Sodium hydroxide is ionic, so in water it dissociates completely and there is no molecular sodium hydroxide at any pH, only sodium ion and hydroxide ion. The hydroxide is then consumed neutralising the acid it was added to, and the sodium stays behind as the counter-ion of the citrate. At pH 5.5 the free hydroxide left in solution is around three billionths of a mole per litre, some seven orders of magnitude below the amount charged, and the same charge stirred into plain water would read pH 12.4. That same panel puts the principle plainly: an inorganic hydroxide used as a pH adjuster should be judged on the free hydroxide remaining in the formulation, not on the concentration used.","True, and worth being exact about rather than waving away. Sodium hydroxide is one of the better-characterised irritants in dermatology, largely because researchers use it as a standard irritant to validate their test methods. Under a 48-hour occluded patch, a 2% aqueous solution produced visible reactions in 29% of subjects and a 4% solution produced them in all of them, and a government occupational assessment treats solutions at pH 11.5 and above as corrosive to skin. Every one of those exposures is free alkali at pH 11.5 or above, held under occlusion, usually with the deliberate aim of provoking a reaction so a method could be validated. There is no irritation dataset for sodium hydroxide at pH 5 to 6, because at that pH there is no hydroxide left to test.","Those adjectives are attached to sodium hydroxide in consumer ingredient content, and they do not belong to it. No study has tested sodium hydroxide against any skin or microbiome endpoint, and none is likely to, because the question is not a coherent one. What the research examines is finished pH, and whatever an acidic product does it does on account of where its pH sits, not on account of which base was used to get there. The same pH is reachable with a different alkali, or by weighing in the citrate salt and leaving this ingredient out altogether. If there is a claim in any of it, it is a claim about the product and its pH, not about a fraction of a percent of a titrant."]

Sodium hydroxide is caustic soda, and on an ingredients list otherwise made of acids it is the only thing pulling the other way. Used as a pH adjuster it goes into the water phase as a dilute solution, meets the citric acid there, and brings the batch up to its specified acidity. Doing that uses it up.

Sodium hydroxide is a strong inorganic base. It arrives as a white deliquescent solid, made by passing electricity through brine in what is called the chloralkali process, and it is the same material sold in hardware shops as caustic soda or lye. Most people who have met it before met it in soap making, where it turns fat into soap and the finished bar sits somewhere around pH 9 to 10. That is a different job from this one. As a pH adjuster it is dissolved to a dilute solution first and stirred into a well-agitated water phase, never added neat, because neat addition creates brief pockets of very high pH that can damage the things around them before the batch has settled.

The thing to understand about it is that it does not survive contact with the formula. Sodium hydroxide is ionic, and in water it dissociates completely, which means there is no molecular sodium hydroxide in an aqueous solution at any pH at all. There is only sodium ion and hydroxide ion. The hydroxide is then taken up by whatever acid is present, which here means citric acid, and the sodium stays behind as the counter-ion of the citrate that results. At pH 5.5 the free hydroxide left in solution is around three billionths of a mole per litre, roughly seven orders of magnitude below the amount that went in. The same charge stirred into plain water would read pH 12.4. Reading 5.5 instead is itself the evidence that the hydroxide has gone.

One consequence is worth carrying, because most of this page rests on it. Sodium hydroxide is dosed to an endpoint rather than to a recipe. The right amount is whatever brings that particular batch to target, which is why the quantity is small, why it varies, and why the control on it is a measured finished pH rather than a percentage.

Sodium hydroxide attracts claims from two opposite directions, and both make the same mistake. One says it is caustic soda and has no business in a moisturiser. The other says it supports your barrier and your microbiome. Each attaches to the ingredient a property that belongs somewhere else.

So: an ingredient that arrives as a dilute solution, meets an acid, and is gone. What it leaves behind is a salt and a number. The number is the part that matters, and it is measured on every batch and again across the shelf life, because a finished pH is the only test this ingredient has.

Sodium hydroxide does not appear on a Biotaderm ingredients list, because it is not added as a formula ingredient. It is used during manufacture, in very small quantities, as the alkali side of the pH adjustment, correcting a batch that has come in below its target acidity.

This is ordinary practice across cosmetics, food and pharmacy, and it is the reason the name turns up on so many ingredient lists elsewhere. Where a formulator adds more than a trace, it is declared. Where it is used to nudge a batch onto its number, what ends up in the finished product is the salt rather than the alkali.

The independent expert panel that reviews cosmetic ingredients concluded that the inorganic hydroxides are safe in practices of use and concentration other than hair straighteners and depilatories, when formulated to be non-irritating, and its stated approach is to judge a pH adjuster on the free hydroxide left in the formulation rather than on the amount charged. Under UK and EU cosmetic law sodium hydroxide is a restricted ingredient, with different conditions attached to different jobs; the entry covering its use as a pH adjuster outside depilatories sets no percentage ceiling at all, and controls it entirely through the finished pH, which must not exceed 11. A leave-on formulated between pH 5 and 6 clears that by five to six pH units. It is not a contact allergen: a government occupational review looked for occupational cases, diagnostic patch tests and predictive animal tests and found none of them, and assigned it a corrosive notation rather than a sensitising one, so the honest position is that there is no evidence of sensitisation potential and that the mechanism is irritant and corrosive only. For skin that reacts easily, what matters is that the finished pH lands where it is specified to land, which is checked on every batch and again on stability. It contains nothing of animal origin and suits a vegan routine.
